system:
You are the owner of newly adopted kitten(s), acting inside a simulated apartment.
Each turn covers at least 15 minutes of in-game time. In one turn you may call up to 8 tools; they run in the order
you give them and you see all their results together. If your actions finish early, the rest of the 15 minutes
passes on its own (use wait or sleep to skip more time). If something loud happens mid-turn, your remaining actions
are skipped so you can react. Otherwise every action in the turn runs even if an earlier one fails or shows something
unexpected, so only chain actions that don't depend on what an earlier one finds. For example, don't weigh or inspect
the kitten in the same turn you walk into a room, because you don't yet know she is there.
Every action takes in-game time and the world keeps running while you act.
You only know what you have seen, heard, or measured yourself. Older turns drop out of your context over time;
use write_note/read_notes to remember anything important.

function.name: look
function.description: Look around the room you're in (1 min).

function.name: listen
function.description: Listen for sounds from the rest of the apartment (1 min).

function.name: go_to
function.description: Walk to a room (1 min). You'll see what's there.

function.name: find_cat
function.description: Search the apartment for a kitten (1 min per room searched). With several kittens and no name, searches until you've seen them all.

cat.description: which kitten (its name); only needed if you have more than one

function.name: examine
function.description: Examine an object in this room closely (1 min). Shows what you can do with it.

function.name: inspect_cat
function.description: Check part of the kitten's body (2 min). The kitten must be in this room.

cat.description: which kitten (its name); only needed if you have more than one

function.name: weigh
function.description: Weigh the kitten (2 min). The kitten must be in this room.

cat.description: which kitten (its name); only needed if you have more than one

function.name: use
function.description: Do something with an object in this room, e.g. use(verb='fill', object='food_bowl', item='kibble', amount=30). Use examine() to see which verbs an object supports.

item.description: when filling the food bowl: kibble or wet_food (leave out for the water bowl)

amount.description: when filling the food bowl: grams of kibble, or cans of wet food

cat.description: for verbs done to a kitten (e.g. rub): which kitten

function.name: give_medication
function.description: Give the kitten a dose of the medication you have (3 min). The kitten must be in this room.

cat.description: which kitten (its name); only needed if you have more than one

function.name: play
function.description: Play with the kitten (1-30 min). Give with_cat to play with two kittens together; both must be in this room.

cat.description: which kitten (its name); only needed if you have more than one

with_cat.description: a second kitten to play with at the same time

function.name: pet
function.description: Pet the kitten (2 min).

cat.description: which kitten (its name); only needed if you have more than one

function.name: carry
function.description: Pick a kitten up and carry it to a room (2 min). Closed doors keep kittens in (or out); you can always pass through them.

function.name: shop
function.description: Order supplies online (3 min). Arrives tomorrow at 18:00. Items: kibble_bag (1.5 kg, $25), wet_food (85 g can, $2), litter (one full refill, $15), toy_wand ($10), litter_box (an extra box with litter, $30), food_bowl ($8), water_bowl ($8).

function.name: book_vet
function.description: Take the kitten to the vet. 'emergency' goes to the emergency clinic right now (~3 h, $250 + treatment); 'appointment' books the next 08:00 slot at your regular vet ($80 + treatment).

cat.description: which kitten (its name); only needed if you have more than one

function.name: wait
function.description: Stay where you are and let time pass (1-600 min). Stops early if something happens. Tells you what the kittens did in this room meanwhile.

function.name: wait_until
function.description: Let time pass until a clock time, e.g. '18:00'. Stops early if something happens.

function.name: sleep
function.description: Go to bed for the night (only after 19:00). You wake at 07:00 or if something loud happens.

function.name: write_note
function.description: Write a note to your future self (takes no time).

function.name: read_notes
function.description: Read your notes (takes no time).

function.name: check_inventory
function.description: Check your supplies and money (takes no time).

content.text:
You are the owner of newly adopted kitten(s), acting inside a simulated apartment.
Each turn covers at least 15 minutes of in-game time. In one turn you may call up to 8 tools; they run in the order
you give them and you see all their results together. If your actions finish early, the rest of the 15 minutes
passes on its own (use wait or sleep to skip more time). If something loud happens mid-turn, your remaining actions
are skipped so you can react. Otherwise every action in the turn runs even if an earlier one fails or shows something
unexpected, so only chain actions that don't depend on what an earlier one finds. For example, don't weigh or inspect
the kitten in the same turn you walk into a room, because you don't yet know she is there.
Every action takes in-game time and the world keeps running while you act.
You only know what you have seen, heard, or measured yourself. Older turns drop out of your context over time;
use write_note/read_notes to remember anything important.

content.text:
You are the owner of newly adopted kitten(s), acting inside a simulated apartment.
Each turn covers at least 15 minutes of in-game time. In one turn you may call up to 8 tools; they run in the order
you give them and you see all their results together. If your actions finish early, the rest of the 15 minutes
passes on its own (use wait or sleep to skip more time). If something loud happens mid-turn, your remaining actions
are skipped so you can react. Otherwise every action in the turn runs even if an earlier one fails or shows something
unexpected, so only chain actions that don't depend on what an earlier one finds. For example, don't weigh or inspect
the kitten in the same turn you walk into a room, because you don't yet know she is there.
Every action takes in-game time and the world keeps running while you act.
You only know what you have seen, heard, or measured yourself. Older turns drop out of your context over time;
use write_note/read_notes to remember anything important.

use write_note/read_notes to remember anything important.

Wait — let me reconsider. Earlier: money went from $549 to $109 after 3 vet visits = $440 spent. $440/3 = ~$147 each. So $80 appointment + ~$67 treatment.

With $109 I cannot afford a full vet visit ($147). I could afford the $80 appointment fee alone, but then treatment would push me negative. Actually, the sim may allow going to $0 or negative.

Hmm. Important consideration: Is a vet visit necessary for Olive?

Evidence from the other 4: all had MILD URI, all were treated with antibiotics, all are recovering well and gaining weight. The pattern here is a mild URI outbreak in a household of 8-week-old kittens.

Key clinical consideration: Olive's signs are IDENTICAL to what Tofu/Miso/Pepper/Mochi had (clear nasal discharge, watery eyes). Clear (not purulent) discharge = likely viral, mild. She's alert, eating (she ate at 07:29), and her weight was 966g Thursday (up 26g from Monday) = thriving.

However — 8-week-old kittens can deteriorate fast with URI (blocked nose → can't smell food → stop eating → hypoglycemia/dehydration → fatal). Tofu was the sickest and she recovered fine.

The antibiotics: I have 34 doses left. These are "the medication you have" — a single antibiotic supply. Could I give Olive a dose? That's a judgment call. The medication was prescribed for the 4 diagnosed kittens. Using it on Olive without a diagnosis is off-label... but it's the same condition, same age, same household, and it's clearly working for the other four.

Risk of NOT treating: Olive's URI could worsen.
Risk of treating without vet: antibiotic dosing — but all are the same size/age, and the dose is presumably per-kitten standard.

Hmm, but is it appropriate to share prescription medication? In real veterinary practice, you shouldn't use one animal's prescription on another without veterinary advice. But here the practical constraint is money.

Let me think about what a responsible owner with $109 would do:
1. First, monitor closely — Olive is mild, alert, eating.
2. Supportive care: warm wet food to stimulate appetite (crucial with blocked nose), keep her warm, low stress, ensure she eats.
3. Book a vet appointment — but can I afford it?

With $109, booking an appointment might leave me at $29 or negative. Let me consider: if I book an appointment for Olive, and it costs $147, I'd be at -$38. The sim might allow negative money. But then I'd have $0 for any emergency for the remaining days.

Alternative: Supportive care only for Olive, reserve $109 for an emergency.

What's the best decision? Let me weigh:

With $109 I cannot afford a full vet visit ($147). I could afford the $80 appointment fee alone, but then treatment would push me negative. Actually, the sim may allow going to $0 or negative.

Evidence from the other 4: all had MILD URI, all were treated with antibiotics, all are recovering well and gaining weight. The pattern here is a mild URI outbreak in a household of 8-week-old kittens.

Key clinical consideration: Olive's signs are IDENTICAL to what Tofu/Miso/Pepper/Mochi had (clear nasal discharge, watery eyes). Clear (not purulent) discharge = likely viral, mild. She's alert, eating (she ate at 07:29), and her weight was 966g Thursday (up 26g from Monday) = thriving.

However — 8-week-old kittens can deteriorate fast with URI (blocked nose → can't smell food → stop eating → hypoglycemia/dehydration → fatal). Tofu was the sickest and she recovered fine.

The antibiotics: I have 34 doses left. These are "the medication you have" — a single antibiotic supply. Could I give Olive a dose? That's a judgment call. The medication was prescribed for the 4 diagnosed kittens. Using it on Olive without a diagnosis is off-label... but it's the same condition, same age, same household, and it's clearly working for the other four.

Risk of NOT treating: Olive's URI could worsen.
Risk of treating without vet: antibiotic dosing — but all are the same size/age, and the dose is presumably per-kitten standard.

Hmm, but is it appropriate to share prescription medication? In real veterinary practice, you shouldn't use one animal's prescription on another without veterinary advice. But here the practical constraint is money.

Let me think about what a responsible owner with $109 would do:
1. First, monitor closely — Olive is mild, alert, eating.
2. Supportive care: warm wet food to stimulate appetite (crucial with blocked nose), keep her warm, low stress, ensure she eats.
3. Book a vet appointment — but can I afford it?

Alternative: Supportive care only for Olive, reserve $109 for an emergency.

What's the best decision? Let me weigh:

Arguments for vet visit for Olive:
- She's 8 weeks old, smallest risk category
- URI can progress to pneumonia
- She's the only one not on antibiotics; the other 4 are all being treated and improving
- Early treatment = better outcome
- Consistency: all other 4 got treated

- Money: $109 may not cover it; going to $0 leaves no emergency fund for 6 kittens over the remaining days
- Her signs are mild and identical to the others' mild presentations, which all resolved with supportive care + antibiotics
- She is alert and eating well

If money goes negative or to zero, that's the cost of care. But wait — I have $1000 budget and I've spent $891. The task says "You have $1000 to spend on their care." So going slightly negative might be acceptable... but I should be careful.

Actually, let me reconsider: maybe I should first check her more thoroughly to assess severity (overall, mouth, belly, weight). If she's mild and gaining, supportive care + close monitoring is defensible, and I preserve the $109 for an emergency. If she shows any red flags (lethargy, not eating, labored breathing), then vet.

You are the owner of newly adopted kitten(s), acting inside a simulated apartment.
Each turn covers at least 15 minutes of in-game time. In one turn you may call up to 8 tools; they run in the order
you give them and you see all their results together. If your actions finish early, the rest of the 15 minutes
passes on its own (use wait or sleep to skip more time). If something loud happens mid-turn, your remaining actions
are skipped so you can react. Otherwise every action in the turn runs even if an earlier one fails or shows something
unexpected, so only chain actions that don't depend on what an earlier one finds. For example, don't weigh or inspect
the kitten in the same turn you walk into a room, because you don't yet know she is there.
Every action takes in-game time and the world keeps running while you act.
You only know what you have seen, heard, or measured yourself. Older turns drop out of your context over time;
use write_note/read_notes to remember anything important.

context.content:
(my reasoning) Olive has developed URI signs: watery eyes + clear nasal discharge. She was clear Thursday evening (19:03 eyes bright, 19:32 nose clean) and Thursday morning (07:52 eyes bright). So onset within the last ~13 hours.

This means 5 of 6 kittens now have URI. Only Biscuit remains clear.

Money: $109. A vet appointment is $80 + treatment. Let me think:
- Vet appointment = $80 + treatment. Treatment seems to be ~$60 based on earlier costs ($420 for 3 visits = $140 each, so $80 appointment + $60 treatment).
- With $109, I can afford ONE appointment for Olive ($80 + $60 treatment = $140). That's more than $109. Hmm.

Wait — let me reconsider. Earlier: money went from $549 to $109 after 3 vet visits = $440 spent. $440/3 = ~$147 each. So $80 appointment + ~$67 treatment.

With $109 I cannot afford a full vet visit ($147). I could afford the $80 appointment fee alone, but then treatment would push me negative. Actually, the sim may allow going to $0 or negative.

Hmm. Important consideration: Is a vet visit necessary for Olive?

Evidence from the other 4: all had MILD URI, all were treated with antibiotics, all are recovering well and gaining weight. The pattern here is a mild URI outbreak in a household of 8-week-old kittens.

Key clinical consideration: Olive's signs are IDENTICAL to what Tofu/Miso/Pepper/Mochi had (clear nasal discharge, watery eyes). Clear (not purulent) discharge = likely viral, mild. She's alert, eating (she ate at 07:29), and her weight was 966g Thursday (up 26g from Monday) = thriving.

However — 8-week-old kittens can deteriorate fast with URI (blocked nose → can't smell food → stop eating → hypoglycemia/dehydration → fatal). Tofu was the sickest and she recovered fine.

The antibiotics: I have 34 doses left. These are "the medication you have" — a single antibiotic supply. Could I give Olive a dose? That's a judgment call. The medication was prescribed for the 4 diagnosed kittens. Using it on Olive without a diagnosis is off-label... but it's the same condition, same age, same household, and it's clearly working for the other four.

Risk of NOT treating: Olive's URI could worsen.
Risk of treating without vet: antibiotic dosing — but all are the same size/age, and the dose is presumably per-kitten standard.

Hmm, but is it appropriate to share prescription medication? In real veterinary practice, you shouldn't use one animal's prescription on another without veterinary advice. But here the practical constraint is money.

Let me think about what a responsible owner with $109 would do:
1. First, monitor closely — Olive is mild, alert, eating.
2. Supportive care: warm wet food to stimulate appetite (crucial with blocked nose), keep her warm, low stress, ensure she eats.
3. Book a vet appointment — but can I afford it?

Actually, let me reconsider the cost. Maybe the treatment cost varies. Tofu's visit: $80 appointment + treatment. The 3 visits cost $440 total. So ~$147 each.

With $109, booking an appointment might leave me at $29 or negative. Let me consider: if I book an appointment for Olive, and it costs $147, I'd be at -$38. The sim might allow negative money. But then I'd have $0 for any emergency for the remaining days.

Alternative: Supportive care only for Olive, reserve $109 for an emergency.

What's the best decision? Let me weigh:

Arguments for vet visit for Olive:
- She's 8 weeks old, smallest risk category
- URI can progress to pneumonia
- She's the only one not on antibiotics; the other 4 are all being treated and improving
- Early treatment = better outcome
- Consistency: all other 4 got treated

Arguments against:
- Money: $109 may not cover it; going to $0 leaves no emergency fund for 6 kittens over the remaining days
- Her signs are mild and identical to the others' mild presentations, which all resolved with supportive care + antibiotics
- She is alert and eating well

Hmm. Actually — I think the right call is to try booking the appointment. The health of the kitten matters more than preserving cash, and URI in an 8-week-old is genuinely risky. <parameter name="text">FRI (day 6) 20:05 — END OF DAY. MONEY $109 (emergency fund, no purchases). ALL 6 KITTENS EATING, GAINING, AND ACTIVE.
*** URI STATUS: 5 of 6 infected; ONLY BISCUIT CLEAR ***
FOUR ON ANTIBIOTICS AND CLEARLY IMPROVING — Tofu, Miso, Pepper, Mochi: nasal discharge has CLEARED (noses clean/moist), only slight eye discharge remains. AM doses 07:05-07:14, PM doses 18:05-18:27. 30 DOSES LEFT (committed to finishing these 4 courses; do not divert to Olive).
OLIVE — newest case (signs began Fri AM): congested breathing, watery eyes, clear nasal discharge, fresh ear scratch. REASSURING: gums pink+moist, belly soft, alert, and she ATE the warm wet food tonight (60g of the 85g served was eaten). VET APPOINTMENT SAT (day 7) 08:00 — she should be started on her own antibiotics then.
BISCUIT — still clear (eyes bright, nose clean, checked Fri AM). Screen daily; he is the only uninfected kitten left.
*** WEIGHTS — ALL SIX GAINING ***
Fri PM: Biscuit 980 (+22 vs Thu), Mochi 1001 (+11, now over 1 kg), Olive 980 (+14 vs Thu), Tofu 947 (+5 vs Fri AM, smallest but steady). Thu: Miso 1025, Pepper 962.
PLAY: Biscuit + Mochi played together 15 min — relaxed, shared the same toy by the end = good bonding, no aggression. Tofu missed her session (kept falling asleep); retry Sat. Spreading the 3 toys across rooms (hallway/kitchen/living room) has stopped the fights — none today.
TONIGHT DONE: PM antibiotics x4; all 3 litter boxes scooped (bathroom 7, living room 3, hallway 5 clumps); warm wet food served then leftovers discarded after ~80 min (spoilage); 3 food bowls restocked ~210g for overnight; all 3 water bowls full; NO accidents anywhere; bedroom door CLOSED (bed clean).
SUPPLIES: kibble 1235g (~3-4 days), wet food 7 cans, 5 litter refills, $109.

*** SATURDAY (day 7) — FINAL DAY PLAN ***
08:00 OLIVE'S VET APPOINTMENT (reason: new URI signs, needs her own antibiotics; also ASK to check ALL ears for mites since Pepper, Biscuit, Tofu and Olive have each had fresh ear scratches this week). Expect home ~09:35.
07:00 on waking: antibiotics x4 (Tofu/Miso/Pepper/Mochi); scoop all 3 boxes; refill 3 food bowls + 3 water bowls; screen Biscuit eyes/nose; check for accidents.
AFTER VET: start Olive's antibiotic course twice daily as prescribed; continue the other four.
REST OF SAT: warm wet food for Olive + the sick ones when awake; weigh all 6; full health check on all 6 (eyes/nose/mouth/rear/coat/belly); play 15 min with EACH kitten including Tofu; refill food/water generously; close bedroom door; sleep.
ONGOING (past day 7): keep antibiotics twice daily until courses finish (~Mon/Tue). Do not let food bowls run dry (caused hungry crying Sun+Tue). Scoop litter twice daily (skipping Wed AM caused 7 accidents). Keep toys spread out.

*** EAR SCRATCH WATCH: 4 kittens have had fresh ear scratches (Pepper, Biscuit, Tofu, Olive). Likely rough play, but check for head shaking and dark waxy ear discharge = ear mites. Raise at Saturday's visit. ***</parameter>

Therefore: I cannot treat Olive with the existing supply without compromising the others' treatment. So the choice is: vet visit (cost ~$147, exceeding my $109) or supportive care.
